purpose: Ethacrynic acid is a 'water pill' that helps your body get rid of extra fluid that has built up, usually due to heart failure, liver disease, or kidney problems. It reduces swelling in your legs, ankles, or belly and can also help lower high blood pressure. Your doctor may also use it when other water pills haven't worked for you.
how_it_works: Your kidneys filter your blood and decide how much water and salt to keep or send out as urine. Ethacrynic acid works by blocking a specific spot in your kidneys called the 'loop of Henle,' telling your kidneys to release more salt and water into your urine. This means you urinate more often, which helps drain the extra fluid from your body and reduces swelling.
common_side_effects: You may urinate much more frequently, especially right after taking the medication. You might feel dizzy, lightheaded, or tired. Low levels of potassium, sodium, or other electrolytes can cause muscle cramps, weakness, or irregular heartbeat. Nausea, stomach upset, and diarrhea can also occur.
warnings: This medication can cause serious hearing loss or ringing in the ears, especially at high doses or if taken with other medicines that affect hearing — tell your doctor right away if this happens. It can cause your potassium levels to drop dangerously low, so you may need to eat potassium-rich foods or take a supplement. Avoid taking it if you have little to no urine output. Tell your doctor about all your other medications, especially other diuretics, blood pressure medicines, or antibiotics like gentamicin. Do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor first.
typical_dosing: For most adults, the starting dose is usually 50 mg taken by mouth once a day with food to reduce stomach upset. Your doctor may slowly increase the dose based on how your body responds, typically ranging from 50 mg to 200 mg per day. It is usually taken in the morning so the extra urination does not disturb your sleep at night. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions.
